title: The son who left (Luke 15:11–24)
hookLine: the younger son spends it all, comes to himself, and the father runs down the road

lines: A FAR COUNTRY, AND A FAMINE.
cards: A man has two sons. The younger one says: give me my share of the inheritance. Now, not when you die.
In that world, and in most of ours, that's close to saying: I wish you were already gone. And the father does it. He divides his property, and the younger son sells up and leaves for a far country.
There he wastes it all, living wildly. Then a famine hits. He takes the only job he can find, feeding pigs, and he's so hungry he'd gladly eat what the pigs are eating.

teach.b: The Douay-Rheims says he was returning to himself; the King James, he came to himself. As if he'd been away from himself, too.
He works it out: my father's hired workers have more bread than they need, and I'm dying of hunger.

teach.h: A SPEECH ASKING FOR A JOB.
teach.b: So he writes a speech in his head: "I will arise, and will go to my father." He'll say: I've sinned against heaven and before you. I'm not worthy to be called your son.
Make me one of your hired workers. He's hoping for a job, not to be a son again. And he starts the long walk home.

teach.h: A GREAT WAY OFF, THE FATHER RUNS.
teach.b: "And when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." A great way off: he'd been watching the road. And he runs.

teach.h: THE ROBE, THE RING, THE CALF.
teach.b: In that culture, a dignified older man didn't run; he'd have to hitch up his robe and show his legs. He reaches his son before the son can reach the village.
The son starts his speech, and never gets to the part about the hired workers. Bring the best robe. A ring for his hand.
Shoes for his feet. Kill the fatted calf.

"Because this my son was dead, and is come to life again: was lost, and is found." Catholics hear this story as the heart of the sacrament of confession: you come with your speech, and the Father runs to meet you.
Pope John Paul the Second built a whole letter on mercy around it.

how: Catholics hear the parable of the prodigal son in Lent and often in preparing for confession, where the penitent comes back and receives absolution; John Paul II's encyclical Dives in Misericordia (1980) meditates on it at length.

games.q: you're the father. far down the road you see the son who took half your fortune and left. what do you do?
o: wait at the door to hear what he has to say.
run down the road to meet him.
send a servant to find out what he wants.
games.why: he runs, falls on his neck and kisses him, then calls for the robe, the ring and the fatted calf.

practice: Think of a relationship where there's distance you helped make: maybe you left, said something, or just went quiet. You don't have to walk the whole road; just picture the first step, a message, a call, an honest sentence.
If you pray, you can bring your own speech to God and notice that you don't have to finish it.

wordCard.voice: riotously. How the younger son spent everything in the far country, before the hunger and the long walk home.

orig.note: Greek: wastefully, recklessly; the word behind living riotously. The son's life in the far country.

carryVoice: Your line: the father runs. The story says the distance is shorter than it looks. Until tomorrow.
